strengths: Well-motivated problem: existing multi-objective test-time alignment methods require known/predefined weights, which is often unrealistic; the paper convincingly argues why robustness to worst-case weighting is desirable.

Solid theoretical foundation: the max-min game is formalized rigorously, existence of Nash Equilibrium is established via minimax theorem, and the reduction to a convex optimization problem over weights with an analytic best-response policy is a clean and non-trivial theoretical contribution (Propositions 3.1-3.2, KKT analysis in Appendix B).

Practical algorithm design: the paper explicitly addresses computational tractability via sample-based approximation of the expectation, reuse of sampled candidates for both weight optimization and policy sampling, and blockwise decoding, resulting in an algorithm with latency comparable to standard controlled decoding baselines (demonstrated empirically in Appendix C.3).

Broad and reasonably thorough experimental evaluation across three distinct datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) with different numbers of objectives (2 to 10), multiple decoding/training baselines (GRPO, DPO, RS, MOD, MO-GRPO, MO-DPO, UNIFORM), and informative ablations over block size B, trade-off parameter λ, and number of objectives.
Insightful qualitative analysis (Figure 5, 7, Appendix C.4) showing how RMOD dynamically reallocates weights across blocks/objectives during generation, adding interpretability to the method.
Alternative no-regret learning solution (Hedge-BR) is derived and connected to the main gradient-based approach, showing conceptual generality of the framework.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single, relatively small/older base model (gemma-2-2b-it) and small/older reward models (GPT2-large-based reward models for HH), raising concerns about whether the reported gains would hold for larger, more capable LLMs and stronger, more modern reward models; no scaling study across model sizes is provided.

Evaluation relies entirely on automated reward-model scores and a worst-case win-rate metric derived from these same (or highly correlated) reward models used to train the value functions; there is no human evaluation, and no analysis of potential reward hacking/over-optimization against the value function proxies, which is a known risk in reward-guided decoding.

The empirical margin between RMOD and the UNIFORM baseline is sometimes fairly small (e.g., UltraFeedback win rates hovering around 55-62% vs. UNIFORM ~50-55%, Figure 4a), and statistical significance (confidence intervals/variance across seeds) is not consistently reported, making it hard to assess robustness of the claimed improvements.

The headline claim of 'outperforming baselines up to 20%' appears to reference a best-case/cherry-picked comparison point rather than a systematic average improvement, which could overstate the general effectiveness of the method.

The practical algorithm introduces multiple approximations (Monte Carlo estimate of the expectation over z, reuse of sampled candidates instead of exact best-response sampling) whose approximation error is not empirically quantified or bounded, leaving a gap between the theoretical guarantees (Nash Equilibrium, convexity) and what is actually implemented.

Value function training uses a simple CD-FUDGE-style regression to final-response rewards, which is known to be a noisy training signal; the paper does not study value function accuracy or its impact on the quality of the resulting robust weights.

Only one alternative solver (no-regret Hedge-BR) is derived in the appendix, but no empirical comparison against it or against other standard robust/distributionally-robust optimization baselines from the RL literature is provided, limiting understanding of whether the proposed gradient-descent-on-logits approach is actually the best practical choice.

The setup assumes a fixed, discrete set of objectives with reward models available at inference time; scalability and reliability concerns as the number of objectives grows (as shown in Figure 6, both RMOD and UNIFORM degrade) are acknowledged but not deeply investigated or mitigated.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical formulation of robust multi-objective decoding as a minimax game, proves existence of a Nash Equilibrium, shows the game reduces to a convex optimization over weights with an analytic best-response policy, and provides full proofs (including KKT analysis of optimal weight behavior) in the appendix.

A practical, low-latency variant (blockwise sampling-based approximation with iterative weight updates) is proposed to make the theoretical algorithm tractable, and the authors empirically show it incurs minimal additional latency compared to non-robust controlled decoding baselines.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across three datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) with several baselines (DPO, GRPO, Rewarded Soup, MOD, UNIFORM) and multiple ablations (block size, λ, number of objectives), plus a qualitative case study showing how RMOD dynamically reweights objectives during generation.

The connection between the worst-case formulation and Best-of-K/blockwise decoding is clearly laid out, and an alternative no-regret learning solution (Hedge-BR) is discussed and related to the proposed gradient-based method, showing some theoretical breadth.
weaknesses: Evaluation validity is questionable: rewards are computed largely with small, dated reward models (e.g., GPT2-large-based reward models for HH) and the same reward/value function families are used both for training the value functions and for evaluation, raising concerns about circularity and whether gains reflect genuine alignment improvement versus overfitting to the same reward signal.

No human evaluation or use of stronger/independent judges (e.g., GPT-4-as-judge) is included anywhere in the paper, which is increasingly standard for alignment work and would substantially strengthen claims about 'equitable' alignment quality.

Experiments are conducted with a single, relatively small reference model (gemma-2-2b-it), leaving open whether the method's benefits persist at larger, more capable model scales typical of modern LLM alignment research.

The core idea—robust/maxmin optimization over multiple alignment objectives—has already been explored in training-time RLHF settings (e.g., Maxmin-RLHF, Group Robust Preference Optimization, cited in the related work); the contribution here is mainly to port this maxmin idea to inference-time decoding, which is a comparatively incremental step in a fairly crowded controlled-decoding literature (MOD, args, weak-to-strong search, etc.).

The Rawlsian worst-case objective is not critically examined: focusing entirely on the minimum reward can be overly conservative and may sacrifice aggregate quality across objectives; the paper does not analyze this trade-off (e.g., versus Pareto-efficient or other fairness notions) or discuss failure cases where worst-case optimization harms overall utility.

Some baseline results look suspicious (e.g., Rewarded Soup and MOD underperforming even simple UNIFORM decoding), suggesting potential issues with baseline tuning/implementation that undermine the strength of the comparisons and the claimed '20%' improvement, which appears cherry-picked from a specific comparison rather than being representative.

As shown in the paper's own ValuePrism experiments, performance of RMOD (and UNIFORM) degrades notably as the number of objectives grows, raising scalability concerns that are only partially explored and not resolved.

The paper's motivating scenarios (first-time users, noisy preference history, evolving preferences) are not directly tested; there is no experiment demonstrating RMOD's behavior under actual distribution shift or dynamically changing preferences within a conversation, despite this being a central motivation in the introduction.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: robust test-time multi-objective alignment without requiring predefined preference weights, addressing a genuine practical gap in existing weighted-sum decoding approaches.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper formalizes the robust decoding objective as a minimax two-player game, proves existence of a Nash equilibrium, shows the game reduces to a convex optimization over weights, and derives a closed-form best-response policy (Proposition 3.1/3.2), with full proofs in the appendix.

Practical algorithmic contributions to reduce inference-time overhead (Monte Carlo approximation of the expectation, reuse of sampled candidates for direct sampling from the best response, blockwise decoding), with an empirical latency comparison showing negligible overhead versus non-robust controlled decoding (Appendix C.3).

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across three distinct multi-objective datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) with multiple types of baselines (single-objective decoding, UNIFORM, GRPO/DPO fine-tuning, Reward Soup, MOD).

Useful ablations examining the effect of the trade-off parameter λ, block size B, and the number of objectives, along with a theoretical characterization of optimal weight behavior via KKT conditions (Appendix B) that helps interpret why RMOD equalizes rewards across objectives.
Qualitative case study (Appendix C.4) illustrating how RMOD dynamically reallocates weights across objectives during generation, adding interpretability to the method.
weaknesses: Experiments rely on a single, relatively small and dated reference model (gemma-2-2b-it) and old reward models (e.g., gpt2-large reward heads); it is unclear how the method scales to larger, more capable/contemporary LLMs or reward models, limiting confidence in real-world significance.

Evaluation is entirely based on automatic reward model scores and win rates derived from them; there is no human evaluation to validate that improved worst-case reward corresponds to genuinely better or more balanced responses from a human perspective.

Some baselines (RS, MOD, GRPO combinations) perform worse than the simple UNIFORM baseline, which is somewhat counterintuitive and raises questions about whether these baselines were adequately tuned/implemented, weakening the strength of the comparison.

The core idea of robust/minimax formulations for multi-objective alignment is not new in the broader alignment literature (e.g., Maxmin-RLHF, group-robust RLHF); the novelty here is largely in applying this to inference-time/controlled decoding, which is a comparatively incremental extension.
Performance degrades notably as the number of objectives grows (Figure 6), and while the paper acknowledges this, no concrete solution or deeper analysis of scalability limits is offered.

The practical algorithm depends on learned value functions trained via CD-FUDGE-style regression, which can introduce approximation error into both the weight-solving and best-response steps; the paper does not thoroughly analyze the sensitivity of RMOD's robustness guarantees to this value function approximation error.
Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., typographical errors) and dense notation in places make the paper harder to follow than necessary.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: robust alignment across multiple, potentially competing objectives at inference time without requiring pre-specified weights.

Solid theoretical development: formulates the problem as a minimax game, proves existence and characterization of a Nash Equilibrium via the minimax theorem, and reduces the adversarial weight search to a convex (LogSumExp) optimization problem with full proofs in the appendix.

Practical algorithm design that keeps compute overhead low (blockwise decoding, sample-based approximation of the expectation, soft/logit-space gradient updates for weights), with empirical latency shown to be within ~4.5% of standard Controlled Decoding baselines.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three diverse datasets (Anthropic HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) and up to 10 objectives, including reward-based worst-case win rate, LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) evaluation, KL-divergence analysis, and qualitative case studies.

Thorough ablations on key hyperparameters (λ, block size B, number of candidates K, number of objectives), which are consistent with the theoretical predictions about weight sparsity and KL trade-offs.
Provides both a full RMOD algorithm and a distilled SFT version (Distill-RMOD) that retains much of the robustness benefit with substantially reduced inference cost, which is practically appealing.

Comparisons include a reasonably broad set of baselines (CD variants, GRPO/DPO, MO-GRPO/DPO, Rewarded Soups, MOD, best-of-K variants), and additional appendix experiments address alternative explanations (e.g., reward overoptimization in best-of-K).
weaknesses: Experiments rely on relatively small/older models (gemma-2-2b-it as policy, GPT2-large-based reward models) and it is unclear whether the robustness benefits and worst-case reward improvements persist at larger model scales or with stronger, more modern reward models.

The evaluation metric (worst-case reward against small proxy reward models) may not robustly reflect real-world response quality; the appendix itself documents reward overoptimization issues in best-of-K baselines, raising concerns about the reliability of reward-based worst-case win rate as ground truth throughout the main results.

Some baselines (Rewarded Soups, MOD) underperform even the simple UNIFORM decoding baseline, which is surprising and suggests either weak baseline tuning or dataset/setup peculiarities that are not fully explained, weakening the strength of the comparison.

Performance degrades noticeably as the number of objectives grows (ValuePrism experiments), and while this is acknowledged, no mitigation or deeper analysis (e.g., why specific objectives are harder, or how block-size/K should scale) is provided.

The fine-tuning baselines (GRPO/DPO, MO-GRPO/MO-DPO) are not robust multi-objective methods by design (fixed 0.5 weighting), so the comparison to RMOD's adversarial weighting is somewhat apples-to-oranges; the more directly comparable MAXMIN-GRPO robust baseline appears to be described but its results are not clearly reported in the main tables/figures.

The approximation and hyperparameter choices (I iterations, step size η for logit updates, K samples) are given specific values in experiments but not deeply justified or ablated (e.g., sensitivity to I, η is not analyzed), leaving some reproducibility/robustness questions about the practical algorithm.

The paper's core theoretical contribution (minimax game reduces to convex optimization with an analytic best-response policy) is a fairly direct application of the minimax theorem and KL-regularized RLHF-style derivations already used in prior CD literature (Mudgal et al.), somewhat limiting the technical novelty beyond adapting existing recipes to a robust objective.

strengths: The theoretical formulation is clean and internally consistent: casting robust multi-objective decoding as a maximin game between adversarial reward weights and the policy, proving Nash equilibrium existence, and deriving a closed-form best-response policy plus a convex (LogSumExp) optimization for the worst-case weights is a coherent and well-explained derivation with proofs provided in the appendix.

The practical algorithm (block-wise sampling, iterative multiplicative weight updates, reuse of samples to avoid extra forward passes) is reasonably engineered to keep computational overhead low, and this is empirically validated with a dedicated latency study showing <5% overhead versus non-robust Controlled Decoding.

Extensive empirical evaluation spans three datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) with up to 10 objectives, multiple ablations (λ, block size B, K, number of objectives), an LLM-as-judge evaluation to complement reward-model-based scoring, KL-divergence analysis, and qualitative response examples.

The distilled version of RMOD (DISTILL-RMOD) is a nice practical contribution, showing that the robust behavior can be partially transferred into a single-pass model with much lower latency while retaining competitive worst-case performance.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution is a fairly standard application of minimax/robust-optimization machinery (strong duality via the minimax theorem, KL-regularized RLHF best-response policy already established in Mudgal et al. 2023, and simplex-constrained convex optimization) rather than a substantially novel technical insight; the incremental novelty over existing CD and group-robust decoding work (e.g., Yoon et al. 2024) is relatively narrow.

The evaluation relies heavily on comparatively weak/outdated proxy reward models (GPT2-large-based reward models for HH) to both train value functions and evaluate results, which raises concerns about the validity and generalizability of the reported gains despite the LLM-as-judge corroboration on only one dataset.

Only a single small reference model (gemma-2-2b-it) is used across all experiments; there is no evidence the method scales or generalizes to larger or different model families, which limits confidence in the significance of the results.

Several baselines (GRPO, DPO, MO-GRPO, MO-DPO, RS, MOD) are only evaluated on the HH dataset and not on UltraFeedback or ValuePrism, leaving the comparison against strong training-based alternatives incomplete for the larger-scale, more realistic multi-objective settings.

The practical algorithm relies on several approximations (finite-sample estimate of the expectation, learned value functions trained with CD-FUDGE's known approximation error, gradient-based weight updates) whose cumulative effect on the theoretical Nash-equilibrium guarantees is not analyzed, so the gap between the elegant theory and the practical algorithm's actual robustness is unclear.

Performance degrades notably as the number of objectives grows (Figure 5), and worst-case win rate decreases substantially as block size increases (Figure 3a), indicating that the method's benefits are fairly sensitive to hyperparameter choices and objective count, which somewhat undercuts the claimed robustness and practicality.

Some baselines (Reward Soup, MOD) underperforming even the simple UNIFORM decoding baseline is somewhat suspicious and may indicate weak baseline tuning, which weakens the strength of the comparative claims.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: robust alignment to multiple, possibly competing objectives at inference time without needing pre-specified weights.

Strong theoretical foundation: the max-min game is rigorously reduced to a convex optimization problem via minimax duality, with clean closed-form characterization of the best-response policy (Prop 4.1) and Nash equilibrium (Prop 4.2), backed by full proofs in the appendix.

Insightful KKT-based analysis (Section B) showing that optimal weights equalize expected values across active objectives, giving intuitive understanding of the robust solution's behavior and the role of λ in controlling weight sparsity.

Practical, low-overhead algorithm: RMOD approximates the convex program with sampled candidates and soft weight updates, empirically incurring <4.5% latency overhead versus standard Controlled Decoding baselines (Table 2, Appendix C.8).

Extensive empirical evaluation across three diverse datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) with up to 10 objectives, multiple metrics (worst-case reward, worst-case win rate, LLM-as-judge), and many baselines (CD variants, GRPO, DPO, MO-GRPO, MO-DPO, Reward Soup, MOD, best-of-K).
Thorough ablations on block size B, trade-off parameter λ, number of objectives, and KL-divergence budget, which help clarify the algorithm's behavior and trade-offs.
The distilled variant (DISTILL-RMOD) is a nice practical contribution, achieving competitive worst-case performance with substantially lower inference cost/KL divergence than blockwise decoding.

Qualitative examples (Appendix C.9) and weight-trajectory visualizations (Figures 6-7) provide interpretable evidence that RMOD dynamically reallocates focus to the weakest objective during generation.
weaknesses: All main experiments use a single, relatively small reference model (gemma-2-2b-it); it is unclear whether the robustness gains and the low-latency claims hold for larger, more capable LLMs.

Performance of both RMOD and UNIFORM degrades noticeably as the number of objectives grows (Figure 5/9), and the paper only partially investigates why (order-reversal ablation) rather than proposing mitigations, leaving open how RMOD scales to realistic high-dimensional objective settings.

The quality of RMOD's guarantees depends heavily on the accuracy of learned value functions (CD-FUDGE-style approximations); the paper does not thoroughly analyze value-estimation error or its propagation into the worst-case weight computation.

The K-sample Monte-Carlo approximation to the expectation in the convex program (Eq. 7→9) lacks a finite-sample theoretical guarantee connecting the approximate weights ŵ* to the true optimal w*, despite the convexity emphasis in the main text.

Some baselines (Reward Soup, MOD) underperform even simple UNIFORM decoding, which, while informative, raises questions about whether these baselines were tuned/implemented under comparable conditions to RMOD.

Worst-case win rate as the primary metric may favor conservative/hedging behavior; a deeper discussion of the trade-off between worst-case robustness and average-case utility (beyond a few ablation figures) would strengthen the practical case for RMOD.
